paper.title: Education, Birth Order and Family Size
paper.code_data_availability: 'The authors were granted an exemption to publish their data because access to the data is restricted. …

registers.role: sample frame / treatment (family size and birth order) / outcome (educational attainment) / controls (age, sex, parental education and age) / linkage (mother ID, father ID)

linkages: children are linked to their mother and father through the mother ID and father ID in IDA; families are defined as sets of children born to the same mother
parents are located in IDA and parental characteristics (education, age) are merged on to the children-data
only children for whom both parents could be located in IDA are retained

sample.universe: all individuals in Denmark aged 25-74 in 2006 recorded in IDA with non-missing mother and father IDs whose parents were both alive, aged 15-74 and present in the IDA files at some point during 1980-2006
sample.unit_of_observation: child (step 1 and Table 4); family (step 2, Tables 5-8 and B1-B5)
selection_rules: select all individuals in IDA in 2006 with non-missing mother ID and father ID (the children-data); all outcome measurements are taken in 2006
locate both parents in IDA and merge parental characteristics; retain only children where both parents are located
compute family size and assign birth orders
retain only children aged 25 or above in 2006, to ensure completed education
exclude families with children aged 0-14 in 2006, to ensure completed fertility
exclude families in which at least one member (a child or a parent) has missing education data
exclude families where the mother was below 17 or above 49 when giving birth
exclude families containing siblings with different fathers
remove individuals that are part of multiple-birth instances, retaining an indicator for a multiple birth in the family and the parity at which it occurred
family size and birth order are recorded before the individual-level selection criteria are imposed
exclude single-child families from the estimation
sample.n_observations: 1,278,510 individuals in 596,292 families in the estimation samples (single-child families excluded); 1,438,994 individuals in 756,776 families in the analysis data; 2,361,083 individuals in 1,220,477 families before the selection criteria

construction_notes: the outcome is years of education; the analysis data mean is 12.8 years with a standard deviation of 2.8 (Table 1, p. 47)

the dependent variable of the second step is the family-level average years of education net of the effects of age, sex and the average birth order effect, obtained as the fixed effects from the first-step regression (equation (14))
demographic controls are unrestricted indicators for mother's and father's education and five-year-interval indicators for mother's and father's age
family size is treated as completed fertility; families with N = 1 are excluded and N = 2 is the reference case
in the non-linear family size specifications the family size effects are restricted to be constant for families with N >= 6
the variance-covariance matrix of the two-step estimator is obtained by block-bootstrapping at the family level with 100 repetitions; Table 4 reports standard errors clustered at the family level

Minimum Eigenvalue Statistics (Stock and Yogo, 2005) are reported for every 2SLS specification: 15,260.9 and 15,825.5 (twins at last birth), 28,151.6 and 28,156.6 (twins at any parity), 2,657.7 (non-linear family size profile)
Table 1 reports 1.7 siblings on average and a twins-in-family indicator mean of 0.01; Table 2 reports the family size distribution (50.3% two-child families; average 2.5 children)

claims.statement: Table 4 Column (1): the estimated effect of family size on child's education is -0.283 years of education per additional child (OLS, statistically significant).

definition.value: Completed family size N_j: the number of children born to the same mother, entered linearly. Family size is computed after linking children to both parents in IDA and is recorded before the individual-level selection criteria are imposed, so that it represents completed fertility. Families with one child are excluded.

timing.value: completed fertility, fixed at the family level; measured from the 2006 IDA extract

definition.value: Years of education completed by the child, from IDA; all outcome measurements are taken in 2006 and only children aged 25 or above in 2006 are retained so that the measure represents completed education.

timing.value: measured in 2006, at age 25 or above (completed education)

units.value: years of education per additional child

magnitude.interpretation: As expected, the coefficient on family size is negative and implies that an additional child decreases schooling by a little more than a quarter of a year.

estimand.target_population: children aged 25 or above in 2006 in Danish families with at least two children

population.description: Children aged 25 or above in 2006 in the Danish IDA register with non-missing mother and father IDs and both parents locatable in IDA, excluding single-child families and individuals who are part of a multiple birth
subgroups_defined: families with only boys, only girls, and mixed gender families (not reported)
population.selection: All individuals in IDA in 2006 with non-missing mother and father IDs whose parents could both be located in IDA; children aged 25 or above in 2006; families with children aged 0-14 excluded; families with missing education data, mother below 17 or above 49 at birth, or siblings with different fathers excluded; individuals who are part of a multiple birth removed; single-child families excluded. These restrictions reduce the sample from 2,361,083 individuals in 1,220,477 families to 1,438,994 individuals in 756,776 families, and to 1,278,510 individuals in 596,292 families once single-child families are dropped.

identification.source_of_variation: cross-sectional variation in completed family size and birth order across Danish families, with no exogenous variation claimed

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the included controls, family size (and birth order) are uncorrelated with the unobserved family-level determinants of children's education, i.e. with the family effect xi_j of (11).
key_assumptions.supported_by: no supporting evidence is offered: the paper calls the procedure naive and states that it ignores any endogeneity issues, and later attributes the birth order coefficients to family-specific unobservable factors

key_assumptions.assumption: Family size and birth order are deterministically related, so the endogeneity of family size spills over to birth order; the OLS specifications do not address this dual endogeneity.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated in the discussion of the two-step strategy (p. 45)

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection: family size and birth order are recorded before the individual-level selection criteria are imposed, and families with children aged 0-14 in 2006 are excluded, so that the family size measure represents completed fertility; children must be aged 25 or above in 2006 so that education is completed.
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper lists the selection criteria and states the purpose of each (p. 47)

implies_edges.from: sample: completed fertility and completed education (children aged 25+ in 2006, no children aged 0-14)

key_assumptions.assumption: Individuals who are part of a multiple birth are removed from the individual-level sample (birth order is undefined for them), retaining only an indicator for the multiple-birth occurrence and the parity at which it occurred.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated as a selection criterion (p. 47)

implies_edges.from: sample: individuals who are part of a multiple birth excluded

threats_discussed: family size reflects parents' fertility choices and the size of a family and its birth order configuration are deterministically related (dual endogeneity)
endogenous within-family reallocation of resources in response to a twin birth may bias the estimated average family size effect towards zero (Rosenzweig and Zhang, 2009)
twins at the last birth could endogenously affect subsequent fertility
truncation makes the raw twin-at-parity-k indicators correlated with the family fixed effect, invalidating their use as instruments
family-specific unobservable factors could drive the negative OLS birth order coefficients
the empirical analysis abstracts from the spacing/timing of children
robustness_checks: linear and non-linear (indicator) birth order profiles (Table 4 Columns (3), (6), (8); Table 6)
linear and non-linear family size profiles (Table 5 versus Table B1 and Table B5)
family-size-specific birth order profiles (Table 7; Tables B4 and B5)
two instruments: twin birth at the last birth and twin birth at any parity
second-step regressions with and without family-level demographic controls
Minimum Eigenvalue Statistic reported for every 2SLS specification (Stock and Yogo, 2005 critical values)
block-bootstrapped standard errors at the family level (100 repetitions)
Kodde-Palm joint inequality tests and one-sided z-tests of Propositions 2 and 3 (Tables 8, B2, B3)
unresolved_confounders: the roles of child endowments, parental preferences and human capital costs in determining birth order effects cannot be separately identified
the spacing/timing of children is not accounted for
family-specific unobservable factors that affect both completed family size and children's education (addressed only in the family fixed effect and instrumental variable specifications)

estimator.value: OLS

estimation.specification: Equation (11) estimated by OLS on the child-level data, controlling for indicators for age and sex only; no family fixed effects (Table 4, Column (1))
estimation.clustering: standard errors clustered at the family level

mediators_claimed: lower parental resources per child
within household substitution of resources across birth orders

heterogeneity.finding: in more flexible specifications both the family size effect and the composite family size effect increase (in absolute value) with the size of the family (Tables B1 and B5)
results for families with only boys, only girls and mixed gender families were produced but are not reported (available upon request)

ambiguities: baseline_mean/outcome_sd are the mean and standard deviation of the outcome in the analysis data (Table 1, p. 47); the paper prints no control-group or pre-period mean, and none exists in this cross-section.

evidence.how: The paper prints no control-group or pre-period mean of the outcome; the mean (12.8) and standard deviation (2.8) of years of education in the analysis data from Table 1 are recorded instead, as the only printed scale for this outcome.

value.as_printed: hij = α + ι′iδ + ι′N jβ + ξ j + εij
value.lhs: hij (the human capital of a child with birth order i in family j, measured as years of education)
value.parameter_of_interest: β (family size coefficients)

index_sets.over: birth order, i = 1, ..., Nj
families

value.normalisation: Families with N = 1 are excluded and N = 2 is treated as the reference case; birth order indicators are measured relative to the first-born child. In the linear special case the equation becomes hij = α + δi + βNj + ξ j + εij. In Table 4 Columns (1)-(6) the family effect ξ j is not swept out; in the family fixed effect columns it is.

theory_referenced: generalised quantity-quality trade-off (Propositions 2 and 3 of this article)

falsification.condition: rejection of the direct null that the family size effect (Proposition 2) and the composite family size effect (Proposition 3) are non-positive; 'Failure to reject the null constitutes evidence in favor of our model.'

outcomes_examined_not_reported: results for three types of families (families with only boys, families with only girls, and mixed gender families), which the paper says are available upon request from the authors
estimates of the effect of family size using the instrumental variable strategy of Black et al. (2005), which the paper says produce comparable estimates but does not report
